newsitem.title: USA: E-470 deal illustrates bond insurers' competition.
newsitem.headline: E-470 deal illustrates bond insurers' competition.

text.p: Thursday's $811 million E-470 Public Highway Authority, Colo., deal shows just how competitive the municipal bond insurance business has become, some portfolio managers say.
MBIA Insurance Corp will insure the deal, but the Authority had "serious" discussions with one other insurer as well, said Pamela Bailey, the E-470 Authority's chief financial officer.

"We had more than one bond insurer who was discussing insuring this deal with us, so MBIA was definitely not the only (insurer) who thought this was an insurable deal," Bailey said. She declined to name the other insurer.
MBIA also declined to comment.

"I'm just surprised that they can get insurance on it to be honest with you," Jan Terbrueggen, a vice president and portfolio manager who runs a Colorado fund for Nuveen Flagship, said. "It just underscores how much more ravenous the insurance companies have become for business. They wouldn't touch this thing a couple of years ago."

The E-470 project is a toll highway on the eastern perimeter of the Denver Metropolitan Area. The first segment of the four-segment project opened to traffic in June 1991. The design-build contract calls for the total project to be complete by June 30, 1999, Bailey said.

Arapahoe County, Colo., originally issued $722 million of short-term floating rate bonds for the project in 1986, prior to the E-470 Authority's 1988 creation, she said. The debt was remarketed on a fixed-rate, long-term basis in 1995.
Thursday's offering was tentatively priced by a syndicate led by Lehman Brothers. The top yield on the current coupon portion of the issue was 5.35 percent in 2026.
Moody's Investors Service on Monday rated Thursday's sale Baa3, which one analyst there described as "just a refinement" of the Baa rating it assigned in 1995.

"Since the initial rating in August 1995, the (project) has made considerable construction progress, and remains on schedule for a Summer 1999 opening," Moody's release said. "During the past two years Denver's economy has outperformed the orginial projections."
Most proceeds from Thursday's deal will go to refund debt, Bailey said.

If the authority refunds everything possible, the refunding component could total roughly $604 million, she said Wednesday. Moody's release cited the "added flexibility gained from the roughly $72 million in present value savings from the current offering that will refund the outstanding senior debt."

John Wyszynski, an analyst for Aquila Management Corp's Tax-Free Fund of Colorado, said the deal needs to attract institutional investors because "it's not a name that has the best reputation in the state" with retail investors.
Having insurance will make "a huge difference" in broadening the deal's acceptance among institutions, he said.
Along with ever-compressing spreads between high quality and lesser grade paper, competition among bond insurers continues to be a strong theme in the municipal market, Wyszynski said.
"(Insurers) still claim their underwriting standards are at no-loss standards, but taking on the credit risk that we've seen them take that's obviously not the case," he said.
"I think what happened is that everybody except for FGIC went public, and they really need to keep up their premiums," Wyszynski said.
Bill Ahern, portfolio manager of the Eaton Vance Colorado Municipal Bond Fund, said Eaton Vance is currently reviewing the deal.

"Quite frankly we've always been a little bit iffy on the credit itself," Ahern said, adding, "It's a little surprising to us that they would get insurance, that they would be qualified for insurance."
Ahern said while he has only recently taken over the Colorado fund, what strikes him most is the lack of "any sort of structure, any sort of convexity" in Colorado.

Given that underlying credit is questionable and spread compression has reduced compensation buyers get for assuming greater risk, the deal should offer more yield than typical insured paper, Ahern said.

"The only way I'd look at it is if it offered something to the fund besides another five basis points in yield for another insured bond," he said. "You can always find another insured bond, what you need is structure in that state."
